top3.headline: Isomorphic Labs raises $5B to put AI to work on drug design
top3.whyItMatters: Big money now backs AI that does research, which can reshape how whole industries innovate.

top3.headline: Google hands free life-admin agents to hundreds of millions of people
top3.whyItMatters: Mass-market agents will reset what customers expect from every service they use.

top3.headline: Open models now carry about 30% of enterprise AI tokens
top3.whyItMatters: Most companies already use several model providers, so dependence on one lab is fading.

items.title: Gemini Tasks expands free to hundreds of millions in six countries
items.takeaway: Sundar Pichai says Tasks in Gemini, powered by Gemini 4 Hydrogen, is expanding free of charge to hundreds of millions of people in six countries to hand off everyday life admin.
items.soWhat: Consumers will soon expect agents that finish chores, and your customers will bring that expectation.

items.title: Meng To builds a walkable Shinjuku night scene in one HTML file
items.takeaway: Meng To built a Shinjuku night-scene 3D site in three.js: one HTML file, no 3D models, all built in code, walkable with WASD, with time of day and seasons.
items.soWhat: Rich 3D experiences now fit in a single file, so small teams can try immersive ideas cheaply.

items.title: Nathan Benaich: AltaAres wins most lots in NATO counter-drone framework
items.takeaway: Nathan Benaich says AltaAres won six of 16 lots in NATO's counter-drone framework, more than any other supplier, so allied countries can buy its systems without another tender. He believes the team can build a global leader in autonomous defense.
items.soWhat: Early backers see autonomous defense as a real market, with procurement doors now opening.

items.title: Isomorphic Labs raises $5B to speed up AI drug design
items.takeaway: Demis Hassabis announces $5B in funding for Isomorphic Labs to accelerate AI drug design and its mission to 'Solve All Disease'.
items.soWhat: Capital is flowing to AI that does science, not chat, so watch your sector's research pipeline.

items.title: Matt Pocock tests giving agents strictly constrained versions of tools
items.takeaway: Matt Pocock's experiment: if too much choice is bad for agents, build an extremely constrained version of the tools you like. For example, the agent may use React but all state must live in Zustand or useReducer.
items.soWhat: Fewer choices can make agent code more predictable, so set house rules before scaling agents.

items.title: Matt Pocock's prompt: have an agent trial XState v6 in a PR
items.takeaway: Matt Pocock's prompt of the day asks an agent to research the XState v6 beta, find the gnarliest problem in your app it could help with, build a proof of concept in a draft PR and verify it.
items.soWhat: Agents can now trial new libraries against your real code, so evaluations get cheaper.

items.title: Meng To rates Emil's skills among the best for UI design
items.takeaway: Meng To points to Emil's skills as among the best for UI design, animations and interactions, with a link in his post.
items.soWhat: Reusable design skills raise the floor for AI-built interfaces, so check what your team uses.

items.title: Simon Willison: run agents locally, execute their code in a sandbox
items.takeaway: Simon Willison describes an 'external sandbox' pattern: the coding agent runs on your Mac but executes code in a WebAssembly, QEMU or Apple Container sandbox. He shows demos for Claude Code and Codex.
items.soWhat: Sandboxed execution lets teams say yes to coding agents without handing over the whole machine.

items.title: DeepMind's Alex Imas: lab price wars can keep revenue flat
items.takeaway: a16z posts Google DeepMind's Alex Imas saying extreme price competition between frontier labs in recent months can keep lab revenue flat even as token usage soars.
items.soWhat: Price wars favor buyers, so revisit model costs before signing long contracts.

items.title: ChatGPT for Healthcare adds computer-use agents and 20+ plugins
items.takeaway: OpenAI says ChatGPT for Healthcare now has more capable computer-use agents, stronger clinical answers and 20+ new healthcare plugins. Abridge, Ambience, Cigna and CVS Health are named adopters.
items.soWhat: Regulated industries are putting agents into daily work, so benchmark your own sector's pace.

items.title: Claude Code team: let agents verify their own work
items.takeaway: ClaudeDevs says Claude writes better code when it can verify its work, and that tests, benchmarks and end-to-end runs are now cheap. The team published how it thinks about verification.
items.soWhat: Agent output gets more reliable when checks are built in, so budget for tests, not reviews.

items.title: Claude Code desktop can test apps on iPhone Duo's folding layouts
items.takeaway: Claude Code on desktop now supports iPhone Duo in the iOS simulator, in public beta. Claude can fold and unfold the device to test each layout.
items.soWhat: Agents now test layouts on new devices themselves, cutting manual QA for mobile teams.

items.title: Rauch: your users are now agents, so run evals
items.takeaway: Guillermo Rauch says user interviews give way to evals when users are agents, with evals feeding the engineering loop. He also calls traces the new primitive of software development.
items.soWhat: If agents use your product, evals become your user research, so fund them that way.

items.title: California's attorney general sues OpenAI over AI safeguards
items.takeaway: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI, alleging it built AI models without the safeguards and monitoring needed to protect people, NBC News reports.
items.soWhat: Safeguards and monitoring are becoming legal questions, so document yours before regulators ask.

items.title: Databricks: open models now carry about 30% of enterprise tokens
items.takeaway: Databricks' AI Index of 10,000+ companies: open-source models rose from near zero to about 30% of enterprise tokens in five months. 75% use 2+ model providers. P99 user spend is $700/week vs $2.50 at P50.
items.soWhat: Multi-model is now normal, so plan open models for volume and frontier models for hard work.

items.title: OpenAI gives outside safety labs deep access to internal models
items.takeaway: OpenAI is working with Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire on embedded assessments, giving outside experts deep access to internal models and systems to investigate alignment and test safeguards.
items.soWhat: Independent checks on frontier models are expanding, which gives buyers more evidence to weigh before trusting them.

items.title: Perplexity puts 10,000 GPUs toward an automated AI researcher
items.takeaway: Perplexity's new Frontier Research effort will put at least 10,000 GPUs on multi-agent orchestration and continual learning, and says it will publish evals and papers and open source models and tooling.
items.soWhat: A product company is now training its own research agents, widening frontier work beyond the big labs.

items.title: Pocock: remove nuance from agents' choices to avoid slop
items.takeaway: Matt Pocock highlights a talk by @poteto at AIE Code, 'nuance tends to lead to slop', and says to design APIs and automated checks that remove nuance from agent decisions, such as banning useEffect.
items.soWhat: Agents do better with firm rules and automated checks than with judgment calls left open.

items.title: Meng To builds a Dark Souls-style browser game in 3 days
items.takeaway: He used Three.js, Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, Seedream 5.0 Pro and Tripo 3D, and shared prompts in a 10-part thread.
items.soWhat: Small teams can now prototype 3D game ideas in days, with the workflow public.

items.title: Tavi Costa: the US-China yield gap is the key macro divergence
items.takeaway: He shares a chart of US and China 10-year yields and calls the gap the most important divergence between two superpowers funding an AI arms race.
items.soWhat: Borrowing costs shape how long each superpower can keep funding its AI build-out.

items.title: Nathan Benaich: AI infrastructure security is increasingly precarious
items.takeaway: Nathan Benaich says inference providers and their bare-metal suppliers are increasingly precarious on security, and sees room for a company to fix it.
items.soWhat: Ask your inference vendors how they secure the hardware layer beneath your models.

items.title: Meng To shares a 3D workflow using Tripo3D, Blender and Claude
items.takeaway: From Kamome Ashizawa's write-up: give Claude three reference images and a backstory, with CLAUDE.md and planning subagents.
items.soWhat: 3D asset work now runs through agent harnesses, not only modeling tools.

items.title: Garry Tan: Fable 5.2 costs 2.8x more per solved coding task
items.takeaway: On 52 Claude Code tasks, Fable 5.2 solved 82.7% vs 84.6% for Opus 5.5, at 2.80x the cost per solved task.
items.soWhat: Keep the cheaper model as default until harder tasks show a real gap.

voices.quote: Claude writes better code when it can verify its work. Checks that used to be expensive, like tests, benchmarks, and end-to-end runs, are now cheap.
I believe Traces are the essential new primitive of software development and agentic evolution.
Fable 5.2 is the first model that consistently ignores unimportant feedback.
as models get more capable, we see them moving from doing tasks towards pursuing goals
On 52 coding tasks in Claude Code 2.1.322, Fable 5.2 solved about as many (82.7% vs 84.6%) but cost 2.80x as much per solved task.
